set1.q: A 34-year-old man on a mountain trek at high altitude wakes frequently at night. His tent partner notices that his breathing speeds up and then stops, over and over, without snoring. He has no heart failure and takes no medications. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Panic attacks are on the differential for nighttime awakenings. Tell: a repeating cycle of hyperventilation and apnea during sleep at high altitude is the breathing pattern of central apnea, not an anxiety episode.

Nocturnal asthma is on the differential for nighttime breathing complaints. Tell: the cycle of hyperventilation alternating with apnea, at high altitude, matches both the risk factor and the mechanism of central sleep apnea.

Correct. High altitude is a risk factor for central sleep apnea, in which increased sensitivity to carbon dioxide produces an unstable pattern of hyperventilation alternating with apnea. Frequent awakenings without snoring fit, since snoring is less common than in obstructive sleep apnea.

Obstructive sleep apnea comes from upper airway narrowing and usually brings loud, habitual snoring. Tell: a repeating cycle of fast breathing and then no breathing, at altitude and without snoring, is the central pattern.

set1.q: A 62-year-old woman is diagnosed with obesity hypoventilation syndrome. She has coexisting obstructive sleep apnea, and her awake room-air oxygen saturation is 85% (normal 95-100%). Which feature of her presentation points to a poor prognosis?
opts: About 90% of patients have coexisting obstructive sleep apnea symptoms, so it is the usual picture, not a marker of a worse outcome. Tell: her awake saturation of 85% is the feature linked to poor prognosis.

Correct. Prognosis is poor when there is significant awake hypoxemia at diagnosis and with positive airway pressure therapy. Her awake room-air saturation of 85% is well below normal, and the syndrome already carries high mortality and morbidity, with cardiovascular disease the leading cause of death.

Sex is not the named prognostic marker: male gender is not even a risk factor for the syndrome, and older women make up the sleep-hypoventilation subgroup. Tell: the marker of poor prognosis is significant awake hypoxemia.
Patients may present in their 50s and 60s, so her age is typical, not a prognostic marker. Tell: the feature tied to poor prognosis is significant awake hypoxemia at diagnosis.

set1.q: A 66-year-old man has heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and central sleep apnea. His heart failure therapy has been optimized, and continuous positive airway pressure has failed. Which therapy should be avoided because of his heart failure?
opts: Optimizing heart failure therapy is the cause-directed treatment of central apnea in heart failure, and it is recommended, not avoided. Tell: the therapy that can lower his cardiac output by reducing preload is adaptive servo-ventilation.

Polysomnography is how central sleep apnea is diagnosed, and no heart failure restriction is attached to it. Tell: the hazard in reduced ejection fraction is the preload-lowering effect of adaptive servo-ventilation.

Correct. Adaptive servo-ventilation is the usual step after continuous positive airway pressure fails, but it is not used for every patient, especially in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction: with poor left ventricular function, reducing preload can decrease cardiac output. Cheyne-Stokes breathing can also be protective.

Continuous positive airway pressure is considered first in central sleep apnea, and no reduced-ejection-fraction warning is attached to it. Tell: the safety warning tied to poor left ventricular function belongs to adaptive servo-ventilation.

set1.q: A 58-year-old man with a body mass index of 41 kg/m2 has loud snoring and daytime sleepiness. His awake arterial carbon dioxide pressure is 49 mm Hg (normal 35-45). Which sleep study should be avoided in his evaluation?
opts: Polysomnography with continuous nocturnal carbon dioxide monitoring is the gold standard for obesity hypoventilation syndrome. Tell: it is the study he should have; the one set aside in awake hypoventilation is the home kit.
An in-laboratory polysomnogram is the study used when awake hypoventilation is present. Tell: it is recommended for him; the kit is the study to avoid.
A positive airway pressure titration sets the device pressure once the diagnosis is known, a legitimate later step. Tell: the study set aside in awake hypoventilation is the at-home kit.

Correct. In patients with awake hypoventilation a polysomnogram is used, not an at-home kit, and home kits assess obstructive sleep apnea without other sleep disorders. His awake carbon dioxide of 49 mm Hg is awake hypoventilation, and the gold standard for suspected obesity hypoventilation is polysomnography with continuous carbon dioxide monitoring.

set1.q: A 39-year-old woman with no sleep complaints asks, at a community health fair, to fill out a sleep apnea screening questionnaire to learn whether she has obstructive sleep apnea. What should she be told?
opts: A high score confirms the disease

A questionnaire sorts patients into low, intermediate or high risk; the diagnosis comes from a polysomnogram showing 5 or more obstructive events per hour with symptoms, or 15 or more. Tell: a score names a risk group, not a diagnosis.
It is the routine community screen

Screening questionnaires should not be routinely used in the community. Tell: the questionnaire's place is preoperative evaluation of people without a known diagnosis who may be at risk for perioperative complications, not community screening.

Correct. Screening questionnaires should not be routinely used to screen for obstructive sleep apnea in the community, and the questionnaire cannot serve as a true, accurate screening tool in asymptomatic patients. Its value lies in highly symptomatic patients in high-risk settings, such as a preoperative evaluation.
A low score rules the disease out

The questionnaire is not an accurate screen in people without symptoms, so a reassuring score in a woman with no complaints does not settle the question. Tell: its use is limited to highly symptomatic patients in high-risk settings such as preoperative evaluation.

set1.q: A 56-year-old woman with a body mass index of 44 kg/m2 has daytime hypersomnolence, loud snoring and dyspnea on exertion. Awake on room air, her arterial carbon dioxide pressure is 54 mm Hg (normal 35-45). Her chest radiograph, thyroid function tests, pulmonary function tests and toxicology screen show no other cause of hypoventilation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Central sleep apnea is a pattern of apneas without respiratory effort during sleep, tied to heart failure, stroke, opioids or altitude. Tell: none of those is described for her, and her defining finding is awake hypercapnia with obesity.

Narcolepsy is listed with the other causes of daytime sleepiness. Tell: it does not explain an awake arterial carbon dioxide pressure above 45 mm Hg, which with a body mass index above 30 points to obesity hypoventilation syndrome.

Correct. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion made when obesity (body mass index above 30) and awake alveolar hypoventilation (arterial carbon dioxide pressure above 45 mm Hg) are present and alternative causes of hypercapnia are excluded. Her 44 kg/m2, 54 mm Hg and negative workup meet all three.

Her snoring and hypersomnolence fit obstructive sleep apnea, which coexists in about 90% of these patients, but it does not account for awake hypercapnia of 54 mm Hg. Tell: awake carbon dioxide above 45 in an obese patient, other causes excluded, defines obesity hypoventilation syndrome.

set1.q: A 45-year-old man with obstructive sleep apnea has a body mass index of 36 kg/m2. He asks what he can do himself, in addition to using his positive airway pressure device. Which risk modification fits him?
opts: Sleeping on his back each night

Positional therapy keeps the patient on his side, with a sleep belt or sleep shirt, when events occur while supine. Tell: lying on his back is the position the therapy avoids; for his obesity the self-care step is weight loss.
A nightly sedative to deepen sleep

Sedatives are a risk factor for obstructive sleep apnea, and the advice is to avoid them. Tell: a sedative works against him; diet and exercise for weight loss is the change that addresses his body mass index of 36.
An evening glass of wine to relax
Alcohol is a risk factor, and avoiding alcohol and other sedatives is a named risk modification. Tell: relaxing with wine works against him; diet and exercise for weight loss target his obesity.
Diet and exercise for weight loss

Correct. Obesity heads the risk factors for obstructive sleep apnea, and diet and exercise for weight loss is a named risk modification, together with avoiding alcohol and other sedatives. Bariatric surgery for weight loss may also be helpful.

set1.q: A 58-year-old man with a body mass index of 37 kg/m2 has an awake arterial carbon dioxide pressure of 51 mm Hg (normal 35-45). He has not yet had a chest radiograph, pulmonary function tests, thyroid function tests or a toxicology screen. What must happen before obesity hypoventilation syndrome can be diagnosed?
opts: Confirm a body mass index above 35

The obesity criterion for this diagnosis is a body mass index above 30, and his 37 already meets it. Tell: 35 is the screening questionnaire's body mass index item; what he lacks is exclusion of other causes.

Bilevel positive airway pressure is first-line therapy, with weight loss, for the syndrome with sleep-related hypoventilation, once it is diagnosed. Tell: his diagnosis is not yet established, because other causes have not been excluded.

Correct. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion: obesity (body mass index above 30) and awake hypercapnia (arterial carbon dioxide pressure above 45 mm Hg) must be joined by exclusion of alternative causes of hypercapnia and hypoventilation. The workup includes a chest radiograph, pulmonary function tests, thyroid function tests and a toxicology screen.

About 90% of patients have coexisting obstructive sleep apnea symptoms, but obese individuals are screened with or without it, and it is not one of the three criteria. Tell: the missing criterion is exclusion of other causes.

set1.q: A 43-year-old woman with habitual snoring and daytime sleepiness has a home sleep apnea test that does not show obstructive sleep apnea. Her symptoms persist. What is the best next step?
opts: A negative home study does not exclude mild disease, since home kits will not always diagnose it. Tell: her symptoms persist, so the question stays open until a polysomnogram answers it.

Repeating the same kind of study repeats its limits: home kits assess obstructive sleep apnea alone and can miss mild disease. Tell: the polysomnogram is the study that measures severity across sleep stages and positions.

Stimulants such as modafinil treat sleepiness but carry headaches, anxiety and many drug interactions. Tell: she has no diagnosis yet, and treating the symptom would skip the study that could find mild disease.

Correct. At-home kits will not always diagnose mild obstructive sleep apnea; they are most helpful in moderate to severe disease. A negative home study in a woman with ongoing snoring and sleepiness therefore needs a polysomnogram, which can also find other sleep disorders a home kit cannot assess.

set1.q: A 50-year-old man has a polysomnogram as part of a research study. He has no sleepiness, fatigue or insomnia, and no one has noted snoring or pauses in his breathing. The study shows 7 predominantly obstructive events per hour. How should this result be interpreted?
opts: Central apnea shows repetitive apneas in the absence of thoracic-abdominal excursion. Tell: his events are predominantly obstructive, and they fall below the diagnostic threshold for a symptom-free patient anyway.
Continuous positive airway pressure is the most effective treatment once obstructive sleep apnea is diagnosed. Tell: his result meets neither diagnostic criterion, so there is no diagnosis to treat.
Criteria for diagnosis are not met

Correct. Without symptoms, the diagnosis needs 15 or more predominantly obstructive events per hour; 5 or more counts only with a symptom such as sleepiness, fatigue, insomnia, choking or snoring noted by an observer. He has 7 events and no symptoms, so neither criterion is met.

7 events per hour would confirm obstructive sleep apnea only alongside a qualifying symptom. Tell: he has no sleepiness, fatigue, insomnia or observer-noted snoring, so the symptom-free threshold of 15 events per hour applies.

set1.q: A 52-year-old woman with obesity hypoventilation syndrome and obstructive sleep apnea has failed a weight loss program and cannot tolerate positive airway pressure. Which second-line therapy is described as very effective?
opts: Autotitrating positive airway pressure is an obstructive sleep apnea device for patients without significant comorbid conditions, and it is still positive airway pressure. Tell: she cannot tolerate pressure therapy, which moves her to second-line options.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. For patients who fail or do not tolerate first-line therapy, second-line options include tracheostomy with nocturnal ventilation, which is very effective, and bariatric surgery, which may be helpful. She has failed weight loss and cannot tolerate positive airway pressure, so she qualifies.
Bariatric surgery is also second line, but it is described as possibly helpful, not very effective. Tell: the second-line option called very effective is tracheostomy with nocturnal ventilation.

Adaptive servo-ventilation is the step after failed continuous pressure in central sleep apnea, and it is itself a positive airway pressure therapy. Tell: her disease is obesity hypoventilation, and she cannot tolerate pressure therapy.

set1.q: A 51-year-old man is evaluated before elective surgery. He snores loudly and is treated for high blood pressure. He feels rested during the day, and his wife has not seen him stop breathing. His body mass index is 35 kg/m2 and his neck (shirt collar) measures 17 inches. What is his STOP-Bang (snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, pressure, body mass index, age, neck, gender) score?
opts: A score of 4 drops a yes he meets, such as age: 51 is older than 50, so the A item counts. Tell: his yes answers are snoring, pressure, age, neck and male gender, five in all.

Correct. Snoring 1 + tired 0 + observed 0 + treated pressure 1 + body mass index 35 (not more than 35) 0 + age 51 (older than 50) 1 + neck 17 inches 1 + male 1 = 5, the high-risk band (5 to 8). He would also be high risk through 2 yes answers to the first 4 questions plus male gender.

A score of 6 counts his body mass index, but the item asks for more than 35 kg/m2, and exactly 35 is not more. Tell: the B item stays a no at 35; his five yes answers come from snoring, pressure, age, neck and male gender.

A score of 7 adds two items he does not meet: a body mass index of exactly 35 (the item needs more than 35) and daytime tiredness, which he denies. Tell: the total is 5, already in the high-risk band.

set1.q: A 45-year-old woman who takes long-term opioid medications for chronic pain has frequent awakenings, nonrestorative sleep and daytime sleepiness, with little snoring. Her polysomnogram shows repetitive apneas in the absence of thoracic-abdominal excursion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Narcolepsy is listed with the other causes of daytime sleepiness. Tell: it does not explain repetitive apneas on her polysomnogram; apneas without thoracic-abdominal movement are central apneas.

Correct. Repetitive apneas in the absence of thoracic-abdominal excursion are the polysomnogram finding of central sleep apnea: airflow stops because respiratory effort stops. Opioid medications are a listed risk factor, and frequent awakenings, nonrestorative sleep and sleepiness with little snoring fit.

In obstructive sleep apnea the airway collapses while the patient still tries to breathe, so the chest and abdomen keep moving. Tell: absent thoracic-abdominal excursion means absent effort, the central pattern.
ruled out by a stated finding

Obesity hypoventilation syndrome requires obesity and an awake arterial carbon dioxide pressure above 45 mm Hg, other causes excluded. Tell: neither is described, and opioids plus apneas without effort point to central apnea.

set1.q: A 68-year-old man with heart failure has insomnia and frequent awakenings, and central sleep apnea is suspected. Which study establishes the diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Central sleep apnea is diagnosed by polysomnography, and at-home testing is not sufficient. The study shows repetitive apneas in the absence of thoracic-abdominal excursion, and heart failure is also a reason to use a polysomnogram rather than a home kit.

At-home testing is not sufficient for central sleep apnea; home kits assess obstructive sleep apnea and not other sleep disorders. Tell: his heart failure adds a second reason for an in-laboratory study.
ruled out by a stated finding

An arterial blood gas measures awake carbon dioxide, the test that follows a serum bicarbonate above 27 when obesity hypoventilation syndrome is suspected. Tell: central apnea is a pattern of events during sleep, shown on polysomnography.

A thyroid-stimulating hormone level is added to a sleep evaluation when hypothyroidism is suspected. Tell: it cannot show apneas; repetitive apneas without thoracic-abdominal excursion are seen on polysomnography.

set1.q: A 35-year-old woman snores loudly. She feels rested during the day, no one has seen her stop breathing, and she is not treated for high blood pressure. Her body mass index is 36 kg/m2 and her neck (shirt collar) measures 14 inches. Using the STOP-Bang (snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, pressure, body mass index, age, neck, gender) questionnaire, which result fits her?
opts: A score of 1 leaves out her body mass index: 36 kg/m2 is more than 35, so the B item is a yes. Tell: her two yes answers are snoring and body mass index, which still sit in the 0-to-2 band.

Correct. Snoring 1 + tired 0 + observed 0 + pressure 0 + body mass index 36 (more than 35) 1 + age 35 0 + neck 14 inches 0 + female 0 = 2, the low-risk band (0 to 2). The body mass index rule needs 2 or more yes answers to the first 4 questions, and she has 1, so she stays low risk.

The body mass index rule moves a patient to high risk only with yes to 2 or more of the first 4 questions (snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, pressure). Tell: snoring is her single yes among the first 4 questions, so the rule is not met and her total of 2 stays low risk.

A score of 3 adds a yes she does not have: she feels rested, has no observed apneas, no treated pressure, is under 50 and has a 14-inch collar. Tell: her total is 2, snoring plus body mass index above 35.

set1.q: A 79-year-old man with untreated obstructive sleep apnea has daytime drowsiness and nocturia. His daughter asks whether treatment is worthwhile at his age. What is accurate?
opts: Correct. Mortality from obstructive sleep apnea is lower in the elderly because they compensate, but they still have drowsiness and nocturia, and both improve with continuous positive airway pressure. Treating him targets the symptoms that affect his daily life.

Lower mortality in the elderly does not make treatment pointless: drowsiness and nocturia persist and improve with continuous positive airway pressure. Tell: the benefit at his age is relief of those symptoms.
His apnea mortality exceeds a younger man's
Mortality from obstructive sleep apnea is less in the elderly, because older patients compensate. Tell: the problem at his age is persistent drowsiness and nocturia, not a higher death rate.
Nocturia is unrelated to his apnea
Nocturia is a listed symptom of obstructive sleep apnea, and in the elderly it persists and improves with continuous positive airway pressure. Tell: both of his complaints trace back to the apnea.

set1.q: A 76-year-old man with moderate obstructive sleep apnea has no teeth and wears full dentures. He cannot tolerate his continuous positive airway pressure mask and asks about a mouthpiece instead. Which option should be avoided?
opts: Correct. An oral appliance is not effective in patients who have no teeth (or in severe obstructive sleep apnea). He is edentulous, so the mouthpiece he asks about is the option to avoid, even though he cannot tolerate his mask.

Radiofrequency ablation is used in mild to moderate obstructive sleep apnea when continuous positive airway pressure cannot be tolerated, which describes him. Tell: his lack of teeth limits the oral appliance, not this procedure.
A nasal expiratory resistance device uses his own breathing to produce expiratory positive airway pressure and does not depend on teeth. Tell: the option tied to having teeth is the oral appliance.

Positional therapy with a sleep belt or sleep shirt keeps the patient on his side and fits events that occur when supine. Tell: missing teeth do not limit it; the oral appliance is the option that needs them.

set1.q: A 60-year-old man with long-standing untreated obstructive sleep apnea declines therapy. Which cardiovascular effect is expected from his untreated disease?
opts: Arrhythmias increase in untreated obstructive sleep apnea, alongside a 3- to 6-fold risk of sudden cardiac death at night. Tell: untreated disease adds rhythm problems rather than protecting against them.

Correct. The cardiovascular effects of untreated obstructive sleep apnea include increased sympathetic tone, bradycardia, increased blood pressure variability, increased arrhythmias and an increased risk of aortic aneurysms and aortic dissections.

Blood pressure variability increases in untreated obstructive sleep apnea; it does not fall. Tell: the listed cardiovascular increases are sympathetic tone, blood pressure variability, arrhythmias and the risk of aortic aneurysm and dissection.

Sympathetic tone is increased in untreated obstructive sleep apnea, not reduced. Tell: the cardiovascular list pairs increased sympathetic tone with more blood pressure variability, more arrhythmias and more aortic dissection risk.

set1.q: A 58-year-old man with loud snoring, witnessed apneas and daytime sleepiness is seen for evaluation before elective surgery. He has never been tested for sleep apnea. Which property makes the STOP-Bang (snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, pressure, body mass index, age, neck, gender) questionnaire suited to this visit?
opts: The questionnaire is singled out for the highest sensitivity among the questionnaires, the property that suits catching at-risk patients before surgery. Tell: its strength is not missing people at risk, which is sensitivity, not specificity.
It confirms the diagnosis before surgery

A questionnaire estimates risk; obstructive sleep apnea is confirmed on a polysomnogram, with 5 or more obstructive events per hour plus symptoms, or 15 or more. Tell: the score places him in a risk group and does not replace the sleep study.

Severity is measured during a sleep study: a split-night polysomnogram records the first 2 hours of sleep to determine severity. Tell: the questionnaire gives a low, intermediate or high risk of having the disease, not a grade of disease he has.

Correct. The questionnaire has been used as a preoperative evaluation tool for people without a known diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnea who may be at risk for perioperative complications, and it has the highest sensitivity among the questionnaires. A highly symptomatic patient in a high-risk setting is where it has value.

set1.q: A 56-year-old man is seen for evaluation before elective knee surgery and has no known sleep disorder. His wife says he snores loudly enough to be heard through closed doors and has seen him stop breathing during sleep. He denies daytime tiredness. He is treated for high blood pressure. His body mass index is 33 kg/m2 and his neck (shirt collar) measures 16.5 inches. What is his STOP-Bang (snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, pressure, body mass index, age, neck, gender) score?
opts: A score of 4 drops two yes answers, such as age and neck: 56 is older than 50, and a 16.5-inch collar meets the 16-inch item. Tell: he meets three of the four Bang items (age, neck, male), on top of three yes answers to the first 4 questions (snoring, observed apnea, pressure).

A score of 5 misses one yes answer, most often the neck: the questionnaire counts a collar of 16 inches / 40 cm or larger for anyone, so 16.5 inches scores 1. Tell: the neck item has a single cut-off, 16 inches, whatever the patient's sex.

Correct. Snoring 1 + tired 0 + observed apnea 1 + treated pressure 1 + body mass index 33 (not more than 35) 0 + age 56 (older than 50) 1 + neck 16.5 inches (16 or larger) 1 + male 1 = 6. A score of 5 to 8 places him in the high-risk group for obstructive sleep apnea before his surgery.

A score of 7 adds a point for body mass index, but the item asks for more than 35 kg/m2, and his 33 does not qualify. Tell: being obese is not enough for the B item; it needs a body mass index above 35, and his tiredness item is also a no.

set1.q: A 52-year-old woman has severe obstructive sleep apnea on polysomnogram. She finds her mask uncomfortable and asks whether an oral appliance would work as well. What should she be told?
opts: It is not effective in severe disease

Correct. An oral appliance is not effective in severe obstructive sleep apnea or in patients without teeth. Her disease is severe, so the appliance is not a substitute; continuous positive airway pressure remains the most effective treatment for her.
It is the most effective option
Continuous positive airway pressure is the option named most effective, not the oral appliance. Tell: for her severe disease the appliance is not effective at all, so it cannot match the mask.
It works if she sleeps on her back
Sleeping supine is the position positional therapy avoids, keeping the patient on her side when events occur supine. Tell: no sleeping position makes an appliance effective in severe disease.
It equals the mask if worn nightly
Nightly use does not change the limit: the appliance is not effective in severe obstructive sleep apnea. Tell: her severity, not how often she would wear it, rules the appliance out.

set1.q: A 47-year-old man's polysomnogram shows repeated episodes, each 10 seconds or longer, of slowed, shallow, restricted breathing. Airflow is reduced but does not fall by 90%. How are these episodes classified?
opts: An obstructive apnea is a fall in airflow of 90% or more for at least 10 seconds with continued respiratory effort. Tell: his airflow stays above that threshold, so the episodes are hypopneas whatever the effort channel shows.

A central apnea has no airflow and no respiratory effort, because the brainstem stops signaling. Tell: he keeps breathing, slowly and shallowly, so neither airflow nor effort has stopped during these episodes.
ruled out by a stated finding
A mixed apnea has no airflow, with effort absent at first and resuming during the latter part of the event. Tell: his airflow is reduced, not absent, so there is no apnea here to classify as mixed.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A hypopnea is slowed, shallow, restricted breathing that occurs repeatedly during sleep in episodes of 10 seconds or longer. An apnea needs a fall in airflow of 90% or more for at least 10 seconds, which his episodes do not reach, so these are hypopneas.

set1.q: A 71-year-old man had a stroke last year. His wife reports loud snoring and pauses in his breathing during sleep, and a home sleep apnea kit has been ordered. What is the best next step?
opts: Stimulants such as modafinil treat sleepiness and need caution in cardiovascular conditions. Tell: no diagnosis has been made, and the decision in front of you is which sleep study to order after a stroke.
Change the order to a polysomnogram

Correct. Stroke is one of the conditions in which a polysomnogram is used instead of an at-home kit. Stroke is also a risk factor for central sleep apnea, and at-home testing assesses obstructive sleep apnea and is not sufficient for central apnea, so the order should change.
Proceed with the home kit as ordered

A home kit can serve uncomplicated suspected obstructive sleep apnea, but stroke is listed among the conditions that call for a polysomnogram. Tell: his stroke, not his snoring, decides the type of study.
ruled out by a stated finding

Continuous positive airway pressure is the most effective treatment once obstructive sleep apnea is diagnosed. Tell: he has no diagnosis yet, and his stroke also raises the question of central apnea, so a polysomnogram comes first.

set1.q: A 54-year-old man with a body mass index of 39 kg/m2 has loud snoring and daytime sleepiness. His awake arterial carbon dioxide pressure is 43 mm Hg (normal 35-45), and no other cause of hypoventilation has been found. How do his results measure against the criteria for obesity hypoventilation syndrome?
opts: Not met: carbon dioxide not above 45

Correct. The diagnosis needs all three: obesity (body mass index above 30), awake alveolar hypoventilation with an arterial carbon dioxide pressure above 45 mm Hg, and exclusion of other causes. His body mass index of 39 qualifies, but 43 mm Hg is not above 45, so awake hypoventilation is not shown.
Met: obesity with snoring is enough

Snoring is an obstructive sleep apnea symptom found in about 90% of patients with the syndrome, but symptoms are not specific. Tell: the diagnosis turns on awake hypercapnia above 45 mm Hg, and his 43 falls short.
Met: his body mass index exceeds 35

The obesity criterion is a body mass index above 30, which his 39 meets, but obesity alone does not make the diagnosis. Tell: 35 is the screening questionnaire's body mass index item; what is missing here is a carbon dioxide above 45 mm Hg.
Not met: body mass index is too low
His body mass index of 39 is above the cut-off of 30, so the obesity criterion is met. Tell: the criterion he misses is awake hypoventilation, since 43 mm Hg is not above 45.

set1.q: A 61-year-old woman with a body mass index of 43 kg/m2, hypersomnolence and a raised serum bicarbonate is being evaluated for obesity hypoventilation syndrome. Which test is the gold standard for her?
opts: Sleep study with carbon dioxide monitoring

Correct. Polysomnography with continuous nocturnal carbon dioxide monitoring is the gold standard for obesity hypoventilation syndrome. Following carbon dioxide through the night captures the hypoventilation of the syndrome alongside the obstructive events that coexist in about 90% of patients.
Sleep study with oxygen saturation alone

Oxygen saturations feed the screening features, such as an overnight lowest saturation under 80%, but they do not measure carbon dioxide. Tell: the gold standard adds continuous nocturnal carbon dioxide monitoring to polysomnography.

A home kit assesses obstructive sleep apnea and is set aside when there is awake hypoventilation. Tell: the gold standard for this syndrome is polysomnography with continuous carbon dioxide monitoring.

An awake arterial blood gas shows the carbon dioxide above 45 mm Hg that the criteria require, but it is a daytime measurement. Tell: the named gold standard is the overnight study with continuous carbon dioxide monitoring.

set1.q: A 61-year-old man with a body mass index of 47 kg/m2 has facial plethora (facial swelling, puffiness), pedal edema, hepatomegaly and an elevated jugular venous pressure. His serum bicarbonate is 34 mEq/L (normal 22-29) and his awake arterial carbon dioxide pressure is 57 mm Hg (normal 35-45), with alternative causes of hypercapnia excluded. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Central sleep apnea from heart failure

Heart failure is a risk factor for central sleep apnea, but central apnea is a pattern of apneas during sleep, not awake hypercapnia. Tell: his heart failure is right-sided and comes with a raised bicarbonate and awake carbon dioxide of 57 mm Hg, the late picture of obesity hypoventilation.

Obstructive sleep apnea coexists in about 90% of patients with obesity hypoventilation, but by itself it does not explain awake hypercapnia. Tell: an awake arterial carbon dioxide pressure above 45 mm Hg in an obese patient, other causes excluded, is the defining criterion.

Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease is a comorbidity of obstructive sleep apnea, but it does not explain edema, a raised jugular venous pressure or awake hypercapnia. Tell: his hepatomegaly travels with the other signs of right-sided heart failure.

Correct. Many patients with obesity hypoventilation syndrome present late, with right-sided heart failure from pulmonary hypertension (elevated jugular venous pressure, hepatomegaly, pedal edema). Facial plethora and a raised bicarbonate are screening features, and obesity, awake carbon dioxide above 45 mm Hg and excluded alternatives confirm it.

set1.q: A 64-year-old woman's polysomnogram shows events with no airflow. In each, there is no respiratory effort during the first part of the event, and effort resumes during the latter part while airflow is still absent. How are these events classified?
opts: Correct. A mixed apnea has no airflow, with a lack of respiratory effort during the first part of the event and resumption of effort during the latter part. Her events begin like central apneas and end like obstructive ones, which is exactly the mixed pattern.

An obstructive apnea has no airflow with continued respiratory effort throughout, the airway collapsing while the patient tries to breathe. Tell: her events open with no effort at all, which an obstructive event does not show.
ruled out by a stated finding

A central apnea has no airflow and no respiratory effort for the whole event. Tell: effort comes back during the latter part of each of her events, so the event does not stay central from start to finish.
ruled out by a stated finding

A hypopnea is slowed, shallow, restricted breathing in repeated episodes of 10 seconds or longer, with airflow reduced rather than absent. Tell: her airflow is absent, so these are apneas, and the effort pattern makes them mixed.

set1.q: A 78-year-old woman with obstructive sleep apnea has residual daytime sleepiness despite continuous positive airway pressure, and armodafinil is being considered. She has no heart, liver or psychiatric disease. Which approach to its dose fits her?
opts: The same dose as in younger adults
The elderly are singled out for lower doses, so the standard adult dose is not the plan for a 78-year-old. Tell: her age alone is enough to lower the stimulant dose.
Avoiding the drug because of age
Older age calls for a lower dose, not for avoiding the drug. Tell: the conditions that call for caution are cardiovascular, hepatic and psychiatric disease, and she has none of them.
A lower dose than in younger adults

Correct. Stimulants such as modafinil and armodafinil are given at lower doses in the elderly population. At 78, with no cardiovascular, hepatic or psychiatric condition to add caution, she can be considered for the drug at a reduced dose.
A higher dose than in younger adults
Age moves the dose down, not up: lower doses are used in the elderly. Tell: a higher dose would add to listed side effects such as headache, nervousness, dizziness and nausea.

set1.q: A 58-year-old man with obstructive sleep apnea has not been helped by continuous positive airway pressure or an oral appliance. He asks which operation would be a cure. Which procedure is described as a cure for obstructive sleep apnea?
opts: Bariatric surgery for weight loss may be helpful in obstructive sleep apnea, a weaker claim than a cure. Tell: the procedure called a cure is the one that bypasses the site of obstruction, tracheostomy.

Palatal implants are an option in mild obstructive sleep apnea for patients who cannot tolerate continuous positive airway pressure. Tell: they treat mild disease; the cure comes from bypassing the upper airway obstruction.

Radiofrequency ablation is used in mild to moderate disease when continuous positive airway pressure cannot be tolerated. Tell: it is a treatment option; tracheostomy, which bypasses the obstruction, is the one called a cure.

Correct. Tracheostomy is a cure for obstructive sleep apnea because the site of upper airway obstruction is bypassed. Breathing no longer depends on the narrowed upper airway that collapses during sleep.

set1.q: A 72-year-old man with heart failure has central sleep apnea with Cheyne-Stokes breathing (hyperventilation alternating with apnea) on polysomnography. His leg edema is worsening, his heart failure medicines have not been adjusted in a year, and he takes no opioids. What is the first step?
opts: Repeat with a home sleep test
At-home testing is not sufficient for central sleep apnea, and his diagnosis is already made on polysomnography. Tell: the open question is treatment, which starts with his heart failure.

Correct. Central sleep apnea is treated by addressing the underlying cause first, and in heart failure the step is to optimize heart failure therapy. His worsening edema shows his heart failure is not controlled; continuous positive airway pressure is considered afterward, then adaptive servo-ventilation if it fails.

Adaptive servo-ventilation follows a failed trial of continuous positive airway pressure and carries safety concerns in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Tell: his first step is the cause, his poorly controlled heart failure.
Reducing opioids is the cause-directed step when opioid medications drive central apnea. Tell: he takes none; his cause is heart failure, so the step is optimizing its treatment.

set2.q: A 57-year-old man with newly diagnosed obstructive sleep apnea drinks several glasses of wine each night and takes an over-the-counter sedative to fall asleep. Which advice addresses these modifiable risk factors?
opts: Correct. Use of alcohol or sedatives is a risk factor for obstructive sleep apnea, and the risk modifications are to avoid alcohol and other sedatives, along with diet and exercise for weight loss. Both his nightly wine and his sleep aid fall under that advice.
Keep the sedative, stop the wine

Stopping the wine while keeping the sedative leaves one of the two named risk factors in place. Tell: the advice covers alcohol and other sedatives together, so the over-the-counter sleep aid has to go as well as the wine.
Keep the wine, stop the sedative

Stopping the sedative while keeping the wine leaves alcohol, itself a listed risk factor, in his nightly routine. Tell: risk modification names alcohol together with other sedatives, so the wine is part of the problem too.
Take both earlier in the evening

Changing the timing still leaves alcohol and a sedative in his routine, and the risk modification is to avoid them. Tell: the advice is avoidance of alcohol and other sedatives, not rescheduling them around bedtime.

set2.q: A 51-year-old man is newly diagnosed with obesity hypoventilation syndrome and coexisting obstructive sleep apnea. Which referral is part of his patient education and care?
opts: Tracheostomy with nocturnal ventilation is very effective, but it is second line. Tell: he is newly diagnosed and has not failed first-line therapy, so a surgical referral is premature.
The syndrome needs a multidisciplinary approach, and patient education includes referral to a sleep specialist. Tell: managing it without that referral leaves out a named part of his care.

Correct. Patient education for obesity hypoventilation syndrome includes referral to a sleep specialist with proper counseling, and management needs a multidisciplinary approach. First line is a weight loss program with continuous positive airway pressure, the device for the syndrome with obstructive sleep apnea.

Bariatric surgery for weight loss may be helpful, but it is a second-line option for patients who fail or do not tolerate first-line therapy. Tell: at diagnosis, the named referral is to a sleep specialist.

set2.q: A 46-year-old man has habitual snoring and daytime sleepiness. During 6 hours of sleep his polysomnogram records 48 apneas, 42 hypopneas and 36 respiratory effort-related arousals, predominantly obstructive. What is his apnea-hypopnea index?
opts: 7 is the hypopneas alone, 42 / 6, leaving out his 48 apneas. Tell: the index adds apneas and hypopneas before dividing by the hours of sleep, so (48 + 42) / 6 = 15 events per hour.
8 is the apneas alone, 48 / 6, leaving out his 42 hypopneas. Tell: both event types are counted in the numerator, (48 + 42) / 6 = 15, and only the arousals stay out.

Correct. The apnea-hypopnea index is (apneas + hypopneas) divided by total sleep time in hours: (48 + 42) / 6 = 90 / 6 = 15 events per hour. Respiratory effort-related arousals belong to the respiratory disturbance index, not to this one. At 15 or more predominantly obstructive events, the diagnosis is confirmed.
21 adds the 36 respiratory effort-related arousals: (48 + 42 + 36) / 6 = 21, which is his respiratory disturbance index. Tell: the apnea-hypopnea index leaves the arousals out and comes to 15.

set2.q: A 50-year-old woman reports loud snoring and feeling tired most days. No one has seen her stop breathing during sleep, and she is not treated for high blood pressure. Her body mass index is 38 kg/m2 and her neck (shirt collar) measures 15 inches. What is her STOP-Bang (snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, pressure, body mass index, age, neck, gender) score?
opts: A score of 2 leaves out her body mass index: the B item is yes above 35 kg/m2, and 38 qualifies. Tell: she scores snoring, tiredness and body mass index; only her age, neck, sex, pressure and observed apnea items are no.

Correct. Snoring 1 + tired 1 + observed apnea 0 + pressure 0 + body mass index 38 (more than 35) 1 + age 50 (not older than 50) 0 + neck 15 inches 0 + female 0 = 3. The count alone is intermediate (3 to 4), and her 2 yes answers to the first 4 questions plus a body mass index above 35 meet the questionnaire's added high-risk rule.
A score of 4 counts her age, but the item asks for age older than 50, and she is exactly 50. Tell: at 50 the age item is still a no; it turns yes at 51, so her total stays at 3.

A score of 5 adds both age and neck, and neither qualifies: she is not older than 50, and a 15-inch collar is under the 16-inch item. Tell: her three yes answers are snoring, tiredness and a body mass index above 35.

opts: Untreated obstructive sleep apnea raises cardiovascular risks such as hypertension, arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death at night, but the referral named for the sleep disorder is a sleep physician. Tell: he is being evaluated for the apnea itself.

Correct. Patient education for obstructive sleep apnea includes referral to a sleep physician, together with proper counseling. His snoring, witnessed apneas and sleepiness make the diagnosis likely, and confirming it takes a sleep study.

Bariatric surgery for weight loss may be helpful, but it is a surgical option rather than the referral named for a suspected diagnosis. Tell: the named referral is to a sleep physician, with proper counseling.
Maxillomandibular advancement is one of many surgical options for established disease. Tell: he has no diagnosis yet, and the referral named in patient education is to a sleep physician.

set2.q: A 48-year-old man has loud, habitual snoring, unrefreshing sleep, morning headaches and nocturia. His wife has seen him stop breathing and wake gasping. His blood pressure is poorly controlled on two medicines. His neck circumference is 18 inches, and his posterior oropharynx is crowded. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Narcolepsy is listed with the other causes of daytime sleepiness in the differential. Tell: it does not explain witnessed apneas, gasping awakenings and loud snoring, which are events of an airway obstructing during sleep.

Correct. Loud habitual snoring, witnessed apneas, awakening with gasping, unrefreshing sleep, morning headaches, nocturia and poorly controlled hypertension are its history findings, and a large neck and a crowded posterior oropharynx are its examination findings. Narrowing of the upper airway by soft tissue or structure causes it.

Central sleep apnea sounds very similar, with insomnia, frequent awakenings and daytime sleepiness, but snoring is less common and it clusters with heart failure, stroke, opioids or high altitude. Tell: loud habitual snoring and a crowded oropharynx point to an obstructed airway.

Obesity hypoventilation syndrome needs obesity (body mass index above 30) plus awake hypoventilation, an arterial carbon dioxide pressure above 45 mm Hg, with other causes excluded. Tell: nothing here shows awake hypercapnia; his findings are those of an airway that obstructs at night.

set2.q: A 66-year-old woman with a body mass index of 42 kg/m2 has obesity hypoventilation syndrome, confirmed by exclusion. Her husband has witnessed few apneas, and polysomnography with continuous carbon dioxide monitoring shows sleep-related hypoventilation. Which first-line treatment fits her?
opts: Tracheostomy with nocturnal ventilation is very effective, but it is second line, for patients who fail or do not tolerate first-line therapy. Tell: she is just starting treatment and has failed nothing.

Bariatric surgery for weight loss may be helpful, but it sits in second line, after first-line therapy fails or is not tolerated. Tell: first line is a weight loss program plus positive airway pressure.
Weight loss plus bilevel positive airway pressure

Correct. First-line therapy for obesity hypoventilation syndrome is a weight loss program with positive airway pressure, and the device follows the overlap: with sleep-related hypoventilation it is bilevel positive airway pressure. Her few witnessed apneas, older age and female sex fit that 10% subgroup.
Weight loss plus continuous positive airway pressure

Continuous positive airway pressure is the first-line device when obesity hypoventilation coexists with obstructive sleep apnea. Tell: her study shows sleep-related hypoventilation with few witnessed apneas, which calls for bilevel pressure.

set2.q: A 52-year-old man's polysomnogram shows repeated events in which thermistor airflow falls by 90% or more for 15 seconds while chest and abdominal respiratory effort continue. How is each event classified?
opts: A central apnea has no airflow and no respiratory effort, because the brainstem stops sending the signal to breathe. Tell: his chest and abdomen keep moving throughout each event, so effort is present and the event is not central.
ruled out by a stated finding

A mixed apnea opens with no respiratory effort, and effort resumes only during the latter part of the event. Tell: his effort is present from the start of each event to its end, which is the obstructive pattern rather than the mixed one.

A hypopnea is slowed, shallow, restricted breathing in repeated episodes of 10 seconds or longer, short of a near-total stop. Tell: a fall in airflow of 90% or more is near or total cessation of breathing, which defines an apnea.

Correct. An apnea is a 90% or greater fall in airflow on the thermistor lasting at least 10 seconds, and when airflow stops but respiratory effort continues, the apnea is obstructive. The airway collapses while the patient still tries to breathe, the event pattern of obstructive sleep apnea.

set2.q: A 64-year-old man with obesity hypoventilation syndrome asks what most often causes death in people with his condition. What should he be told?
opts: Severe hypoxemic hypercapnic respiratory failure is an end-stage presentation in patients who present late. Tell: the leading cause of death is cardiovascular disease, the direction in which the syndrome progresses.
Driving accidents rise 2.5 times with the daytime sleepiness of untreated obstructive sleep apnea. Tell: the leading cause of death in obesity hypoventilation syndrome is cardiovascular disease.

Insulin resistance is a listed complication of the syndrome, but it is not named the leading cause of death. Tell: cardiovascular disease holds that place, through pulmonary hypertension and right-sided heart failure.

Correct. The leading cause of death in obesity hypoventilation syndrome is cardiovascular disease. Untreated, the syndrome tends to progress, and many patients develop pulmonary hypertension and right-sided heart failure; mortality and morbidity are high.

set2.q: A 70-year-old man with heart failure reports insomnia, frequent awakenings and nocturnal dyspnea. His wife says he rarely snores, and his breathing at night shows Cheyne-Stokes breathing (hyperventilation alternating with apnea). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome needs obesity (body mass index above 30) and awake hypercapnia above 45 mm Hg with other causes excluded. Tell: nothing here shows obesity or awake hypercapnia; his pattern is the heart failure breathing of central apnea.

Panic attacks are on the differential for nighttime awakenings in suspected sleep apnea. Tell: they do not explain a sleeping pattern of hyperventilation alternating with apnea in a patient with heart failure, the risk factor tied to central apnea.

Correct. Heart failure is a risk factor for central sleep apnea, especially through Cheyne-Stokes breathing, hyperventilation alternating with apnea from increased sensitivity to carbon dioxide and a prolonged circulation delay to the carotid chemoreceptors. Insomnia, awakenings and nocturnal dyspnea fit, and snoring is less common than in obstructive apnea.

Obstructive sleep apnea brings loud, habitual snoring, and its airway collapses while the patient keeps trying to breathe. Tell: rare snoring with hyperventilation alternating with apnea in a man with heart failure points to a central cause, the brainstem signal failing.

set2.q: A 44-year-old man with obstructive sleep apnea has respiratory events on polysomnogram that occur when he sleeps on his back and not when he lies on his side. He wants a measure to add to his care. Which therapy targets this pattern?
opts: Correct. Positional therapy fits when events occur in the supine position: a sleep belt or sleep shirt keeps him lying on his side. His events are confined to back-sleeping, the exact pattern it addresses.
Nasal steroids treat nasal congestion and inflammation from allergic rhinitis in patients with obstructive sleep apnea. Tell: he has no nasal symptoms; his events depend on his body position.

Palatal implants are for mild obstructive sleep apnea when continuous positive airway pressure cannot be tolerated. Tell: nothing says he cannot tolerate pressure therapy, and his events are tied to position.

Tracheostomy is a cure because it bypasses the site of upper airway obstruction, but it is a surgical airway. Tell: his events depend on body position, which a sleep belt or shirt addresses without surgery.

set2.q: A 52-year-old woman with loud snoring and fatigue has an 8-hour polysomnogram that records 40 apneas, 32 hypopneas and 40 respiratory effort-related arousals. What is her respiratory disturbance index?
opts: 4 is the hypopneas alone, 32 / 8. Tell: the respiratory disturbance index counts apneas, hypopneas and respiratory effort-related arousals together, which gives 112 / 8 = 14.
5 is a single event type over the night, 40 / 8, either the apneas or the arousals. Tell: this index sums all three event types before dividing by the 8 hours of sleep, giving 14.
9 is the apnea-hypopnea index, (40 + 32) / 8, which leaves out the arousals. Tell: the respiratory disturbance index adds the 40 respiratory effort-related arousals, (40 + 32 + 40) / 8 = 14.

Correct. The respiratory disturbance index is (apneas + hypopneas + respiratory effort-related arousals) divided by total sleep time in hours: (40 + 32 + 40) / 8 = 112 / 8 = 14 events per hour. The arousals are obstructive airflow reductions that are neither apneas nor hypopneas.

set2.q: A 55-year-old man with long-standing untreated obstructive sleep apnea has blood tests drawn. Which laboratory change is expected from his untreated disease?
opts: Correct. The endocrine effects of untreated obstructive sleep apnea include increased C-reactive protein, cortisol and amyloid, with decreased growth hormone and prolactin. Proinflammatory cytokines also rise, and they improve with continuous positive airway pressure.
Growth hormone falls in untreated obstructive sleep apnea. Tell: the markers that rise are C-reactive protein, cortisol and amyloid; growth hormone and prolactin are the two that drop.
Prolactin decreases in untreated obstructive sleep apnea, along with growth hormone. Tell: of the listed endocrine effects, the increases are C-reactive protein, cortisol and amyloid.
Cortisol increases in untreated obstructive sleep apnea, alongside C-reactive protein and amyloid. Tell: the hormones that decrease are growth hormone and prolactin, not cortisol.

set2.q: A 48-year-old woman with newly diagnosed obesity hypoventilation syndrome asks to start a weight-loss medication instead of a diet and exercise program. What should she be told?
opts: Medication follows failed diet and exercise

Correct. Medications for obesity hypoventilation syndrome are reserved for those who fail diet and exercise measures. First line is a weight loss program with lifestyle changes (diet, exercise, behavioral modification) plus positive airway pressure, within a multidisciplinary approach.
First line is a weight loss program plus bilevel or continuous positive airway pressure. Tell: medications are second line, used for those who fail diet and exercise measures.
Positive airway pressure is part of first-line therapy along with weight loss, and medication is not offered as its substitute. Tell: drugs enter the plan later, after diet and exercise fail.

Bariatric surgery and medications both appear among the second-line options for patients who fail first-line therapy. Tell: the condition attached to medication is failure of diet and exercise, not prior surgery.

set2.q: A 52-year-old man who takes long-term opioid medications has central sleep apnea confirmed on polysomnography. He has no heart failure and lives at sea level. Which step treats the underlying cause?
opts: Adaptive servo-ventilation is the step after continuous positive airway pressure fails, not the opening move. Tell: the treatment sequence starts with the underlying cause, which for him is his opioid medication.
Optimizing heart failure therapy is the cause-directed step when heart failure drives central apnea. Tell: he has no heart failure; his listed cause is opioid medication.
ruled out by a stated finding

Stimulants such as modafinil are used for sleepiness in obstructive sleep apnea, with cautions and many drug interactions. Tell: a stimulant leaves the cause untouched; reducing opioids treats what is driving his central apnea.

Correct. Central sleep apnea is treated first by addressing the underlying cause, and when the patient takes opioid medications, the step is to reduce the opioids. After that, continuous positive airway pressure is considered, and adaptive servo-ventilation if it fails.

set2.q: A 60-year-old man has central sleep apnea after a stroke. His heart function is normal, he takes no opioids and he lives at sea level. A trial of continuous positive airway pressure has failed. What is the next therapy to consider?
opts: Bilevel positive airway pressure is first-line, with weight loss, for obesity hypoventilation syndrome with sleep-related hypoventilation. Tell: central sleep apnea that fails continuous pressure moves to adaptive servo-ventilation.

Correct. In central sleep apnea, continuous positive airway pressure is considered first, and if it fails, adaptive servo-ventilation is next: it monitors breathing patterns in real time and delivers and adjusts pressure as needed. With normal heart function he lacks the reduced ejection fraction that makes it unsafe.

Reducing opioids is the cause-directed step when the patient takes opioid medications. Tell: he takes none, so there is no opioid to reduce; his next step follows the failed trial of continuous pressure.
ruled out by a stated finding

Autotitrating positive airway pressure is an obstructive sleep apnea option for patients without significant comorbid conditions. Tell: the step named after continuous pressure fails in central apnea is adaptive servo-ventilation.

set2.q: A 50-year-old woman with a body mass index of 41 kg/m2 and obstructive sleep apnea is being evaluated, and her clinician's suspicion of obesity hypoventilation syndrome is low to moderate. Her serum bicarbonate is 31 mEq/L (normal 22-29). What is the next step?
opts: Correct. When suspicion is low to moderate, a serum bicarbonate above 27 means a higher chance of obesity hypoventilation syndrome and the need for an arterial blood gas. Her 31 mEq/L crosses that line, and the gas measures the awake arterial carbon dioxide pressure the diagnosis requires (above 45 mm Hg).
Repeating the bicarbonate delays the step its result already triggers: above 27, the chance of the syndrome is higher and an arterial blood gas is needed. Tell: her 31 mEq/L is already above 27.

A home kit assesses obstructive sleep apnea, which she already has, and is set aside when awake hypoventilation is a concern. Tell: the missing measurement is her awake arterial carbon dioxide pressure, which comes from a blood gas.

A raised bicarbonate is a screening clue, not a criterion; the diagnosis needs an awake arterial carbon dioxide pressure above 45 mm Hg and exclusion of other causes. Tell: the bicarbonate decides who gets the blood gas.

set2.q: A 47-year-old man with a body mass index of 38 kg/m2 has obstructive sleep apnea. Which additional finding, with no other cause found for it, should prompt screening for obesity hypoventilation syndrome?
opts: A serum bicarbonate in the normal range
A raised bicarbonate prompts screening, and above 27 it calls for an arterial blood gas. Tell: a value in the normal range is not a trigger; an awake saturation of 94% or less is.

Loud snoring and witnessed apneas are obstructive sleep apnea symptoms, which he already has, and about 90% of patients with the syndrome share them. Tell: screening is prompted by the added features, such as an awake saturation of 94% or less.

Correct. Obese individuals, with or without obstructive sleep apnea, are screened when they have an unexplained awake room-air oxygen saturation of 94% or less or an overnight lowest under 80%, unexplained exertional dyspnea, signs of pulmonary hypertension or right heart failure, facial plethora or a raised bicarbonate. 93% awake qualifies.
The overnight trigger is a lowest saturation under 80%, and 86% does not reach it. Tell: the awake trigger is 94% or less on room air, which is why an awake reading of 93% qualifies.

set2.q: A 46-year-old man with moderate obstructive sleep apnea cannot tolerate continuous positive airway pressure despite several mask changes. Which option is described for his severity and his intolerance of the device?
opts: Adaptive servo-ventilation is considered for central sleep apnea after continuous positive airway pressure fails, and it is itself a positive airway pressure therapy. Tell: his disease is obstructive, and his problem is tolerating pressure therapy.

Modafinil is a stimulant for sleepiness, with headaches, anxiety and many drug interactions. Tell: no severity or device-intolerance indication is attached to it; radiofrequency ablation carries exactly his two.

Correct. Radiofrequency ablation is used in patients with mild to moderate obstructive sleep apnea who cannot tolerate continuous positive airway pressure. His disease is moderate and he cannot tolerate the device, which matches both conditions.

Palatal implants are used in mild obstructive sleep apnea when continuous positive airway pressure cannot be tolerated. Tell: his disease is moderate, beyond the mild range the implants cover; radiofrequency ablation reaches mild to moderate.

set2.q: A 50-year-old man started modafinil for residual daytime sleepiness from obstructive sleep apnea. Two weeks later he develops a widespread rash and feels unwell. Which adverse effect of the drug best fits?
opts: Correct. Listed side effects of modafinil and armodafinil include headaches, nervousness or anxiety, dizziness, nausea, and dermatologic and systemic hypersensitivities. A widespread rash with feeling unwell after starting the drug fits a dermatologic and systemic hypersensitivity reaction.

Nervousness and anxiety are listed side effects, but they are feelings, not a skin eruption. Tell: a widespread rash with systemic illness matches the dermatologic and systemic hypersensitivities listed for the stimulants.

Worsening sleep apnea would bring more sleepiness, snoring or witnessed apneas, the features of the disease. Tell: a new rash after a new drug points to the drug's listed dermatologic and systemic hypersensitivities.
Headache is a listed side effect of modafinil, but it does not produce a rash. Tell: skin involvement with feeling unwell is the hypersensitivity pattern, a separate listed side effect.

set2.q: A 49-year-old man with untreated obstructive sleep apnea drinks no alcohol. An abdominal ultrasound done for another reason shows hepatic steatosis, and he has no edema or jugular venous distension. Which comorbidity of his sleep disorder fits this finding?
opts: Correct. Patients with obstructive sleep apnea have a 2 to 3 times higher prevalence of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. Hepatic steatosis in a man who drinks no alcohol, with no signs of right heart failure, fits that comorbidity.
He drinks no alcohol, which removes an alcohol-related cause. Tell: the liver comorbidity tied to obstructive sleep apnea is the nonalcoholic form, found 2 to 3 times more often in these patients.
ruled out by a stated finding
Liver congestion from right heart failure

Right-sided heart failure from pulmonary hypertension brings elevated jugular venous pressure, hepatomegaly and pedal edema. Tell: he has no edema or jugular venous distension, and his ultrasound shows fat in the liver, not congestion.
ruled out by a stated finding

Obstructive sleep apnea raises the prevalence of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes, but diabetes is a disorder of glucose, not a liver finding. Tell: hepatic steatosis on ultrasound matches nonalcoholic fatty liver disease.

set2.q: A 34-year-old woman with obstructive sleep apnea has seasonal allergic rhinitis, and the nasal congestion makes her positive airway pressure mask hard to use. Which treatment addresses her congestion?
opts: Positional therapy keeps the patient on her side when events occur while supine. Tell: her complaint is nasal congestion from allergic rhinitis, which positioning does not address; a nasal steroid does.

Correct. Nasal steroids are used in patients with obstructive sleep apnea for nasal congestion and inflammation from allergic rhinitis. Treating her congestion targets the problem that is getting in the way of her positive airway pressure therapy.

Modafinil is a stimulant for sleepiness, with headaches, nervousness, dizziness, nausea and many drug interactions. Tell: her problem is congestion from allergic rhinitis, which is what nasal steroids are used for.
Sedatives are a risk factor for obstructive sleep apnea, and the advice is to avoid them. Tell: a sedative would work against her sleep apnea and leave the congestion untreated.

set2.q: A 66-year-old man with heart failure and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has loud snoring, witnessed apneas and daytime sleepiness. His insurer suggests a home sleep apnea kit. Which test should be used instead?
opts: A thyroid-stimulating hormone level is added when hypothyroidism is suspected, and it does not diagnose a sleep disorder. Tell: nothing here suggests thyroid disease; the question is which sleep study his heart and lung disease allow.

Correct. At-home kits suit uncomplicated suspected obstructive sleep apnea, but in significant cardiopulmonary disease a polysomnogram is used, not an at-home kit. His heart failure and chronic lung disease are that comorbidity, and heart failure is also a risk factor for central apnea, which a home kit cannot assess.
Home sleep apnea kit at a later date

Delaying the same study does not remove the problem: at-home kits are set aside in significant cardiopulmonary disease. Tell: his heart failure and lung disease, not the timing, decide that he needs a polysomnogram.
ruled out by a stated finding

A positive airway pressure titration study is used when the diagnosis of sleep-disordered breathing is already known, to set the pressure. Tell: he has no diagnosis yet, so the first study has to establish one.

set2.q: A 54-year-old woman who has taken opioid medications for chronic back pain for years has snoring, frequent awakenings and daytime sleepiness. Which sleep study fits her?
opts: A questionnaire places a patient in a risk group and cannot diagnose; screening tools have value in symptomatic patients in high-risk settings such as preoperative evaluation. Tell: she already has symptoms, and opioid use decides which study she needs.
A titration study sets the device pressure once the diagnosis is known. Tell: she has no diagnosis yet, and her long-term opioid use points to a diagnostic polysomnogram first.

Correct. Long-term opioid use is one of the settings where a polysomnogram, not an at-home kit, is used. Opioid medications are also a risk factor for central sleep apnea, which home kits cannot assess, since they assess obstructive sleep apnea and not other sleep disorders.

Home kits assess obstructive sleep apnea and not other sleep disorders. Tell: her years of opioid use raise the possibility of central apnea and place her on the list of patients who need a polysomnogram instead.

set2.q: A 47-year-old man has obstructive sleep apnea newly confirmed on polysomnogram, with daytime sleepiness and hypertension. Which treatment is the most effective option for him?
opts: A nasal expiratory resistance device uses the patient's own breathing to produce expiratory positive airway pressure, an alternative device. Tell: the option named most effective is continuous positive airway pressure.

Stimulants such as modafinil target sleepiness, carry headaches, anxiety and many drug interactions, and need caution in cardiovascular conditions. Tell: a stimulant treats a symptom, while continuous positive airway pressure treats the obstruction and is the most effective option.

An oral appliance is one of the non-pharmacologic options, but it is not effective in severe obstructive sleep apnea or in patients without teeth. Tell: the treatment named most effective is continuous positive airway pressure.

Correct. Continuous positive airway pressure is the most effective non-pharmacologic treatment for obstructive sleep apnea. It also improves consequences of untreated disease, such as reflux, raised proinflammatory cytokines and, in the elderly, drowsiness and nocturia.

set2.q: A 61-year-old man was diagnosed with obstructive sleep apnea on a sleep study at another center and now needs the pressure on his new device set. Which study is used?
opts: A split-night study first records 2 hours of sleep to determine severity, for a patient still being diagnosed. Tell: his diagnosis is already known, so the study he needs is the titration by itself.

A diagnostic polysomnogram, such as the all-night study used when baseline disease is mild to moderate, measures severity across stages and positions. Tell: he already has a diagnosis; what is missing is the pressure setting.
A home kit tests for obstructive sleep apnea and does not set device pressure. Tell: with the diagnosis known, the open task is titrating the pressure, which is the job of a titration study.

Correct. A positive airway pressure titration is used when the diagnosis of sleep-disordered breathing is already known; it finds the exact air pressure needed to keep his airway open. His diagnosis is established, so a diagnostic study is not repeated first.

set2.q: A 59-year-old man with untreated obstructive sleep apnea declines treatment and asks how the condition affects his heart. Which risk can be raised as much as 6 times in untreated disease?
opts: Driving accidents are 2.5 times more frequent in untreated disease, because daytime sleepiness increases motor vehicle crashes. Tell: that figure is lower and is not a heart risk; 3 to 6 times is sudden cardiac death at night.

Correct. Untreated obstructive sleep apnea carries a 3- to 6-fold risk of sudden cardiac death at night, alongside high mortality from heart failure. The timing is the point: the excess risk falls during sleep, when the apneas occur.
The 3 to 6 times risk of sudden cardiac death in untreated disease is stated for the night, during sleep, when the obstructive events happen. Tell: the figure is tied to nighttime, not to exercise.

Untreated obstructive sleep apnea triples the risk of hypertension (3 times), short of 6 times. Tell: the figure that reaches 6 times, 3 to 6, belongs to sudden cardiac death, and specifically to death at night.

opts: At-home kits are set aside in neuromuscular weakness and in awake hypoventilation or hypoxemia. Tell: she has both, so a home kit is the wrong study even though her snoring and headaches suggest obstructive sleep apnea.
ruled out by a stated finding

Waiting leaves her symptoms and low awake saturation unexplained, while the diagnosis of sleep-disordered breathing rests on a sleep study. Tell: her weakness and hypoxemia call for a polysomnogram now.
A positive airway pressure titration is used when the diagnosis is already known, to set the device pressure. Tell: she has no diagnosis yet; her first study must be a diagnostic polysomnogram.

Correct. Neuromuscular weakness and awake hypoventilation or hypoxemia are both conditions in which a polysomnogram is used instead of an at-home kit. Her room-air saturation of 92% is below normal, and a polysomnogram can also find sleep disorders other than obstructive sleep apnea.

set2.q: A 58-year-old woman with obesity hypoventilation syndrome stopped her positive airway pressure therapy a year ago. She now has exertional dyspnea, an elevated jugular venous pressure, hepatomegaly and pedal edema. Which complication has developed?
opts: Central sleep apnea is a sleep pattern of apneas without effort, with risk factors such as heart failure, opioids and altitude. Tell: her new findings are physical signs of right-sided heart failure, not a sleep event pattern.

Insulin resistance is a listed complication of the syndrome, but it does not produce edema or a raised jugular venous pressure. Tell: those signs, with hepatomegaly, point to right-sided heart failure from pulmonary hypertension.

Correct. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome tends to progress if left untreated, and many patients develop cardiovascular complications, pulmonary hypertension and right-sided heart failure. Elevated jugular venous pressure, hepatomegaly and pedal edema are the listed signs of right-sided heart failure.

Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease is tied to obstructive sleep apnea, but it does not raise the jugular venous pressure or cause pedal edema. Tell: hepatomegaly with those signs is right-sided heart failure.

set2.q: A 52-year-old woman with untreated obstructive sleep apnea has nightly heartburn and symptoms of laryngopharyngeal reflux. Which treatment of her sleep apnea is expected to improve her reflux?
opts: A nasal expiratory resistance device uses her own breathing to produce expiratory pressure, an alternative device. Tell: the reflux of untreated sleep apnea is reported to improve with continuous positive airway pressure.
Positional therapy with a sleep belt

Positional therapy keeps the patient on her side and suits events that occur when supine. Tell: nothing ties her apnea to position, and the treatment shown to improve this reflux is continuous positive airway pressure.

Nasal steroids treat congestion and inflammation from allergic rhinitis in patients with obstructive sleep apnea. Tell: her complaint is reflux, which improves with continuous positive airway pressure.

Correct. 75 to 100% of patients with untreated obstructive sleep apnea have gastroesophageal reflux disease or laryngopharyngeal reflux, driven by decreased intrathoracic pressure, and the reflux improves with continuous positive airway pressure. Treating her apnea treats a cause of her reflux.
